plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a simple three-dimensional drawing of two conducting spheres joined by a wire. A large shaded sphere occupies the upper right of the frame, and a much smaller sphere in the same style sits at the lower left, roughly a third of the diameter of the first. Both are drawn with a soft interior highlight and are ringed by plus signs spaced around their surfaces to indicate positive charge. A thin grey curve sags gently between them, running from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small one and standing for the connecting wire. Each sphere carries a black dot at its center with a short arrow drawn from that dot out to the surface: the arrow in the large sphere is labeled 'R1' and points up and to the right, while the one in the small sphere is labeled 'R2' and points down and to the left. Giving the two spheres markedly different radii while charging both positively is what sets up the comparison. The arrangement, held at a common potential by the wire, is used to relate the surface charge density on each sphere to its radius.

elements: large conducting sphere (radius R1) at upper right, pale blue-grey with soft interior highlight
small conducting sphere (radius R2, about 1/3 of R1) at lower left, same shading style
plus-sign charge markers distributed over each sphere's surface
thin grey curved wire sagging between the spheres, joining the left side of the large sphere to the right side of the small one
black center dot and radius arrow R1 on the large sphere, pointing up-right
black center dot and radius arrow R2 on the small sphere, pointing down-left
labels R1 and R2 beside the arrows
surface charge density readout (sigma1, sigma2) and potential readout (V1, V2) near each sphere

interactions.label: Radius ratio R1/R2
interactions.teaches: Changing the relative radii redistributes the shared charge: the smaller sphere packs its plus signs more densely, showing sigma is inversely proportional to R at common potential

interactions.label: Wire
interactions.teaches: Only when the wire connects the spheres do their potentials equalize (V1 = V2); disconnecting freezes each sphere's charge and lets the potentials differ, clarifying what the conductor enforces
Clicking either sphere highlights its radius arrow and charge-density readout, focusing the comparison between local radius and charge crowding

demo_steps.title: Connected spheres
demo_steps.narration: With the wire connected and R1/R2 = 3, both spheres sit at one potential while the small sphere's plus signs crowd much closer together — sigma2/sigma1 = R1/R2.

demo_steps.title: Equal radii
demo_steps.narration: Set the ratio to 1: the spheres match in size and the charge density becomes uniform and equal on both.

demo_steps.title: Disconnect the wire
demo_steps.narration: Disconnect the wire: each sphere keeps its charge, the potential labels no longer read equal, and the radius slider no longer redistributes charge.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Large sphere radius ~1.5 world units centered at (+2.2, +0.9, 0); small sphere radius ~0.5 units centered at (-2.4, -0.9, 0) — on-screen small sphere diameter is ~1/3 of the large one. Wire: thin grey (#888) CatmullRom curve from the left flank of the large sphere sagging down to the right flank of the small one, dipping ~0.6 units below the straight line between endpoints. Spheres shaded pale blue-grey (#c9cfe8 to #f2f3fa radial gradient) with a soft white specular highlight offset up-left. Plus signs: black crosses on the surface, ~14 on the large sphere and ~7 on the small one at default; count fixed but apparent density scales as charge sharing: Q1/Q2 = R1/R2, so marker count per sphere should be proportional to its share of total charge (Q_i ∝ R_i when connected), making density sigma_i ∝ 1/R_i visible. Radius arrows: black line from center dot to surface, R1 pointing up-right, R2 pointing down-left, with italic labels. Physics: at common potential V = kQ1/R1 = kQ2/R2, hence sigma1/sigma2 = R2/R1. Readouts: show V1, V2 (equal when connected) and sigma1, sigma2.
interactionPlan.notes: Use SphereGeometry with a MeshStandardMaterial plus a subtle radial-gradient sprite or fresnel-ish shading for the soft interior highlight. Plus signs as small cross sprites tangent to the surface, positioned via a Fibonacci-sphere distribution scaled to each sphere's charge share. Wire shown/hidden (or faded with ends lifted) on toggle. Selected sphere gets an emissive rim and its readout panel bolds. Keep both spheres and wire in one scene; update marker counts and readouts reactively on slider/toggle changes.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for radius ratio R1/R2: the learner changes the relative sphere sizes, the plus signs redistribute more densely on the smaller sphere while the wire keeps both at one potential, showing the inverse relationship between radius and surface charge density.

discrepancies: Wire sags downward in a deep catenary curve, while the source wire bows gently upward in a shallow arc
Charge marker counts are tied to charge share, so the small sphere gets very few plus signs; the source shows a comparable density of plus signs on both spheres
Extra σ and V floating labels above/below the spheres do not appear in the source figure
evaluation.notes: A faithful and physically correct rendering of the two connected conducting spheres with rich, pedagogically sound interactions; only minor compositional differences (wire curvature, marker distribution) distinguish it from the source.
action_items: Reduce the wire sag and flip its bow upward so it matches the source's shallow arc
Use near-uniform marker density on both spheres to visually match the source, and let density differences emerge subtly rather than via hard count proportional to Q
Tighten composition so spheres sit on a rising diagonal with the large sphere upper-right, matching the source framing
